angle: how the rich pay less tax legally, 20 lessons from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: How the Rich Pay Less Tax Than You (Legally)

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Here's something that surprises a lot of people. Some of the richest people in America can pay a lower tax rate on their income than a nurse, a teacher or an electrician. And most of the time, it's completely legal. It's not about secret offshore tricks. It's about how the tax code treats different kinds of money. Today I'll show you how it works, and which of those same rules you can use yourself.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the key idea. In the United States, money earned from working is generally taxed at higher rates than money earned from owning investments held for more than a year. Top federal rates on wages reach thirty seven percent. Top rates on long term capital gains are twenty percent, plus a three point eight percent surtax for high earners.

card.note: U.S. federal rates; state taxes vary

scenes.short_hook: A billionaire can pay a lower tax rate than a nurse. Legally.

scenes.text: That single difference explains a lot. Most people's income comes from a paycheck, so most of their money is taxed at ordinary income rates, plus payroll taxes. The very wealthy usually get most of their income from investments and businesses they own, which are often taxed at lower rates, and sometimes not taxed at all until much later. Same country, same tax code, very different results depending on what kind of money you have.
scenes.caption: WORK MONEY VS OWNER MONEY

scenes.text: We'll explore this from three angles. First, the numbers. The specific rules that let wealthy people pay lower rates. Second, the psychology. How the wealthy think about taxes differently from most people. And third, the playbook. The legal tax advantages ordinary people can use, starting this year. Important reminder. This is general education, not tax advice. Tax laws change often, and your situation is unique, so check with a qualified tax professional before acting.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the numbers. And the first lesson is about the two kinds of income.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our numbers. Tax rates and account rules come from the IRS and the Social Security Administration. Research on the taxes paid by the wealthiest Americans comes from reporting by ProPublica and from analysis by the White House Council of Economic Advisers and the Office of Management and Budget. Warren Buffett's figures come from his 2011 New York Times op ed. Rules and thresholds change every year, so always check the latest numbers.
scenes.caption: OUR NUMBERS

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Seven rules in the tax code that work very differently for people who own assets.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number one. The tax code treats two kinds of income differently.
scenes.caption: LESSON 1

scenes.text: Ordinary income includes wages, salaries, tips, interest and short term investment gains. It's taxed on a progressive scale, with federal rates ranging from ten percent up to thirty seven percent for the highest earners. The more you earn, the higher the rate on each additional dollar.
scenes.caption: ORDINARY INCOME: 10% TO 37%

scenes.text: Long term capital gains, meaning profits on investments held for more than a year, and qualified dividends are taxed on a separate, lower schedule. Federal rates are zero, fifteen or twenty percent, depending on your taxable income. High earners may also owe a three point eight percent net investment income tax.
scenes.caption: LONG TERM GAINS: 0%, 15%, 20%

scenes.text: So imagine two people who each have one million dollars of income in a year. One earns it as salary. The other earns it as long term capital gains from selling stock. The salary earner faces the top ordinary rate on much of it. The investor faces a top rate of twenty percent plus the surtax. The investor's tax bill can be dramatically lower.
scenes.caption: SAME INCOME, DIFFERENT TAX

scenes.text: Lawmakers have argued for decades about whether this is fair. Supporters say lower rates encourage investment and avoid taxing money that was already taxed at the corporate level. Critics say it mostly benefits the wealthy. Either way, it's the law, and understanding it helps you make better decisions with your own money.
scenes.caption: A LONG DEBATE

scenes.text: Lesson number two. Growth isn't taxed until you sell.
scenes.caption: LESSON 2

scenes.text: In the U.S. tax system, you generally owe tax on an investment gain only when you sell, which is called realizing the gain. If you buy a stock for ten thousand dollars and it grows to one hundred thousand, you owe nothing on that ninety thousand dollar gain until you sell. On paper you're richer, but for tax purposes, nothing has happened yet.
scenes.caption: NO SALE, NO TAX
scenes.short_hook: Billionaires can watch their fortunes grow for decades without paying tax on it.

scenes.text: For the very wealthy, most of their fortune is often in stock of companies they founded or own. That stock can grow by billions of dollars without any tax, as long as they don't sell. In 2021, ProPublica analyzed IRS data and reported that the twenty five richest Americans paid federal income taxes equal to about three point four percent of their wealth growth from 2014 to 2018.
scenes.caption: ABOUT 3.4% OF WEALTH GROWTH

scenes.text: That figure is controversial, because it compares taxes to wealth growth, not to taxable income, and wealth growth isn't income under current law. But it shows how much of the richest people's gains can stay untaxed for years. A separate 2021 White House analysis estimated the wealthiest four hundred families paid an average federal individual income tax rate of about eight percent when unrealized gains were counted.
scenes.caption: ABOUT 8% BY ONE ESTIMATE

scenes.text: The lesson for regular investors is simple. Holding investments for the long term, instead of constantly selling, lets your money grow without being slowed down by yearly taxes. It's the same rule the wealthy use, and it's available to anyone with a brokerage account.
scenes.caption: YOU CAN USE THIS TOO

scenes.text: Lesson number three. Borrowing instead of selling.
scenes.caption: LESSON 3

scenes.text: If the wealthy don't sell their assets, how do they pay for their lives? One strategy is borrowing. Banks are often willing to lend large amounts to wealthy clients, using their stock or other assets as collateral. And under U.S. tax law, borrowed money isn't income, so a loan isn't taxed.
scenes.caption: LOANS AREN'T INCOME
scenes.short_hook: Why would a billionaire borrow money? Because loans aren't taxed.

scenes.text: This is sometimes called buy, borrow, die. Buy assets that grow. Borrow against them to fund your lifestyle, often at relatively low interest rates. Never sell, so you never realize the gains. The assets keep growing, and the loans are repaid later, often from the estate.
scenes.caption: BUY, BORROW, DIE

scenes.text: This doesn't work for everyone, and it carries real risk. If asset values fall sharply, lenders can demand more collateral or force sales. And interest rates matter. When borrowing costs rise, the strategy becomes more expensive. It works best for people with enormous assets relative to their spending.
scenes.caption: IT HAS REAL RISKS

scenes.text: For ordinary people, the takeaway isn't to borrow against your investments. It's to understand why the wealthy rarely sell assets. They know every sale can trigger taxes, so they treat their best assets as things to keep, not things to cash out.
scenes.caption: THE WEALTHY RARELY SELL

scenes.text: Lesson number four. The step up in basis.
scenes.caption: LESSON 4

scenes.text: Here's the final piece of buy, borrow, die. When someone dies, their heirs generally receive inherited assets with a new cost basis equal to the value on the date of death. That's called a step up in basis. All of the gains built up during the original owner's lifetime can effectively escape capital gains tax.
scenes.caption: THE STEP UP

scenes.text: Here's an example. Someone buys stock for one hundred thousand dollars. Decades later, it's worth five million when they die. Their heirs inherit it with a basis of five million. If they sell right away, they may owe little or no capital gains tax, even though the stock grew by four point nine million dollars.
scenes.caption: $4.9 MILLION GAIN, LITTLE TAX

scenes.text: Large estates may owe federal estate tax, but only above a very high exemption, which was more than thirteen million dollars per person in recent years, and the amount is set by Congress and changes over time. Most families never pay federal estate tax at all.
scenes.caption: ESTATE TAX HAS A HIGH EXEMPTION

scenes.text: The step up applies to regular families too. A home or stock portfolio passed to children can also receive a step up. That's why estate planning isn't just for the rich. A simple conversation with an estate attorney can save heirs a lot of money.
scenes.caption: IT APPLIES TO FAMILIES TOO

scenes.text: Lesson number five. Payroll taxes hit workers harder.
scenes.caption: LESSON 5

scenes.text: Most workers pay payroll taxes on top of income tax. The Social Security tax is six point two percent of wages, and Medicare tax is one point four five percent. Your employer pays a matching amount. If you're self employed, you generally pay both halves yourself.
scenes.caption: 7.65% FROM EVERY PAYCHECK

scenes.text: But the Social Security portion only applies up to a yearly wage limit, which was about one hundred seventy six thousand dollars in 2025 and usually rises each year. Wages above that limit aren't subject to the six point two percent Social Security tax. So a person earning ten million dollars in salary pays that tax only on the first portion.
scenes.caption: SOCIAL SECURITY TAX HAS A CAP

scenes.text: Investment income, like capital gains and dividends, isn't subject to payroll taxes at all, although high earners may owe the separate three point eight percent net investment income tax. For someone whose income is mostly from investments, payroll taxes are a small factor or none at all.
scenes.caption: INVESTMENT INCOME SKIPS PAYROLL TAX

scenes.text: That means a middle income worker can pay a combined federal rate, income plus payroll, that's higher than someone who earns far more from investments. It's one of the main reasons people say the rich can pay lower rates than the middle class.
scenes.caption: WHY THE MIDDLE CLASS PAYS MORE

scenes.text: Lesson number six. Business owners are taxed on profit.
scenes.caption: LESSON 6

scenes.text: An employee is generally taxed on their gross wages, before most expenses. A business owner is taxed on profit, after legitimate business expenses. Equipment, office costs, business travel, software, and employees' salaries can all reduce taxable profit when they're ordinary and necessary for the business.
scenes.caption: TAXED ON PROFIT

scenes.text: Real estate investors have another powerful tool, depreciation. The tax code allows owners to deduct part of a rental building's cost each year, even if the property is actually rising in value. Depreciation can reduce or even eliminate taxable rental income on paper, although some of it may be recaptured when the property is sold.
scenes.caption: DEPRECIATION

scenes.text: Some business owners also qualify for a deduction on qualified business income, which can reduce taxes on certain pass through business profits. These rules are complex, with limits and conditions, which is why business owners often pay for professional tax help.
scenes.caption: COMPLEX BUT POWERFUL

scenes.text: The key word is legitimate. Deducting personal expenses as business expenses is illegal, and the IRS does audit. But a real side business with real expenses can give ordinary people access to some of the same advantages.
scenes.caption: LEGITIMATE EXPENSES ONLY

scenes.text: Lesson number seven. Carried interest.

card.title: Carried interest
card.sub: a special rule for fund managers

scenes.caption: LESSON 7

scenes.text: Private equity and hedge fund managers often get paid partly through something called carried interest, a share of the fund's profits. Under current law, if certain holding period requirements are met, that share can be taxed as long term capital gains instead of ordinary income.
scenes.caption: CARRIED INTEREST

scenes.text: Critics argue that carried interest is really payment for work, so it should be taxed like wages. Supporters argue it's a return on risk and investment, similar to an ownership stake. Lawmakers have proposed changing it many times, and in 2017 the required holding period was extended to three years for many cases.
scenes.caption: A CONTROVERSIAL RULE

scenes.text: Carried interest affects relatively few people, but it's a clear example of a broader pattern. When income can be labeled as a return on investment instead of a return on labor, it's often taxed at a lower rate.
scenes.caption: LABELS MATTER

scenes.text: For ordinary people, the lesson isn't about carried interest itself. It's that owning assets, through retirement accounts, index funds, real estate or a business, shifts more of your income into categories the tax code treats more favorably.
scenes.caption: OWNERSHIP SHIFTS THE TAX

scenes.text: That's angle one. Two kinds of income, untaxed growth, borrowing, the step up in basis, payroll tax limits, business deductions and carried interest. Now angle two. The psychology.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The wealthy don't just have different rules available. They think about taxes differently. Most people deal with taxes once a year, in April, and try to get it over with. Wealthy people treat taxes as a year round part of every financial decision. Here are seven ways their thinking differs.
scenes.caption: A DIFFERENT MINDSET

scenes.text: Lesson number eight. They think in after tax returns.
scenes.caption: LESSON 8

scenes.text: Most people focus on how much they earn or what their investments return. Wealthy people focus on what they keep. A ten percent return taxed at thirty seven percent leaves about six point three percent. A ten percent return taxed at fifteen percent leaves eight and a half. The after tax number is the one that builds wealth.
scenes.caption: IT'S WHAT YOU KEEP

scenes.text: This changes decisions. Where to hold investments, when to sell, how to get paid, whether to take a raise as salary or equity. Every choice gets evaluated through the question, what's the after tax result?
scenes.caption: EVERY DECISION, AFTER TAX

scenes.text: Regular people can adopt this same habit. When comparing two investments or two jobs, ask what you'll actually keep after taxes, not just the headline number.
scenes.caption: ASK WHAT YOU KEEP

scenes.text: Try this. Look at last year's tax return and calculate your effective tax rate, total tax divided by total income. Knowing that number makes the cost of taxes real.
scenes.caption: FIND YOUR EFFECTIVE RATE

scenes.text: Lesson number nine. They plan all year, not just in April.
scenes.caption: LESSON 9

scenes.text: By the time most people file their taxes, the year is over and most opportunities are gone. Retirement contributions, the timing of sales, charitable gifts, business purchases, all of these usually need to happen before the year ends to count.
scenes.caption: APRIL IS TOO LATE

scenes.text: Wealthy families often meet with tax advisors in the fall to plan moves before December thirty first. Should they sell some investments at a loss to offset gains? Should they make a charitable gift this year or next? Should they convert some retirement money to a Roth?
scenes.caption: FALL PLANNING MEETINGS

scenes.text: You don't need a team of advisors to do a simpler version. A short review in October or November can reveal moves that save real money.
scenes.caption: A SIMPLE FALL REVIEW

scenes.text: Try this. Put a tax planning reminder in your calendar for early November. Check your retirement contributions, your investment gains and losses, and any big expenses coming up.
scenes.caption: NOVEMBER TAX CHECK

scenes.text: Lesson number ten. They see good tax advice as an investment.
scenes.caption: LESSON 10

scenes.text: Many people try to save money by doing complicated taxes themselves. Wealthy people usually see a good tax professional as an investment. If a five hundred dollar consultation saves two thousand dollars in taxes, that's a great return.
scenes.caption: ADVICE AS AN INVESTMENT

scenes.text: For simple situations, a regular paycheck, standard deduction, basic retirement contributions, tax software or free filing programs often work fine. But business income, rental property, stock compensation, big life changes or selling a large investment can justify professional help.
scenes.caption: WHEN HELP IS WORTH IT

scenes.text: Look for credentials like CPA or enrolled agent, and ask how they charge. A good tax professional should save you more than they cost and explain their recommendations clearly.
scenes.caption: CPA OR ENROLLED AGENT

scenes.text: Try this. If your taxes got more complicated this year, book a one time consultation before year end, not after.
scenes.caption: BOOK BEFORE YEAR END

scenes.text: Lesson number eleven. They focus on owning, not just earning.
scenes.caption: LESSON 11

scenes.text: For most people, wealth building starts and ends with a paycheck. But wages are the most heavily taxed kind of income for most people. Wealthy people focus on owning things that grow, like stocks, businesses and real estate, whose gains are often taxed later and at lower rates.
scenes.caption: OWNERS VS EARNERS
scenes.short_hook: The rich don't just earn more. They earn a different kind of money.

scenes.text: That doesn't mean your paycheck isn't important. For most people, it's the engine that makes investing possible. The goal is to turn part of each paycheck into assets, so over time more of your wealth comes from ownership.
scenes.caption: TURN WAGES INTO ASSETS

scenes.text: Over decades, someone who consistently invests can end up with a large portion of their net worth in assets whose growth has never been taxed. That's the same structure the wealthy use, just at a smaller scale.
scenes.caption: THE SAME STRUCTURE

scenes.text: Try this. Look at your net worth and ask what percentage comes from assets that can grow, rather than cash or things that lose value. Aim to increase that percentage every year.
scenes.caption: INCREASE YOUR OWNERSHIP

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you're learning something about taxes that nobody taught you in school, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free, and it helps us keep making these. Now, lesson twelve.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number twelve. They're patient sellers.
scenes.caption: LESSON 12

scenes.text: Sell an investment after eleven months and the gain is generally taxed as ordinary income. Wait just over a year, and it may qualify for lower long term capital gains rates. A few weeks of patience can make a real difference in what you keep.
scenes.caption: WAIT OVER A YEAR

scenes.text: Wealthy investors also avoid unnecessary selling altogether. Every sale can create a tax bill that shrinks the amount left to compound. Holding great assets for decades lets the full amount keep growing.
scenes.caption: HOLD FOR DECADES

scenes.text: Frequent traders face the opposite. Short term gains taxed at higher rates, plus trading costs, can seriously drag down returns, even when their picks are good.
scenes.caption: TRADING CREATES TAXES

scenes.text: Try this. Before selling any investment in a taxable account, check how long you've held it and what the tax would be. Sometimes waiting a bit longer is the smartest move.
scenes.caption: CHECK BEFORE YOU SELL

scenes.text: Lesson number thirteen. They give strategically.
scenes.caption: LESSON 13

scenes.text: Many wealthy people donate appreciated stock instead of cash. If you've held a stock for more than a year and it has grown, donating it directly to a qualified charity can let you avoid capital gains tax on the growth, and, if you itemize, deduct its fair market value, within IRS limits.
scenes.caption: DONATE APPRECIATED STOCK

scenes.text: Some also use donor advised funds, which let them make a large charitable contribution in one year, take the deduction that year if they itemize, and then recommend grants to charities over time.
scenes.caption: DONOR ADVISED FUNDS

scenes.text: People seventy and a half or older can often give directly from an IRA to charity through a qualified charitable distribution, which can count toward required minimum distributions without adding to taxable income. The rules have specific limits, so check the current IRS guidance.
scenes.caption: QUALIFIED CHARITABLE DISTRIBUTIONS

scenes.text: Try this. If you already give to charity, ask whether giving appreciated investments instead of cash would make your gift go further.
scenes.caption: GIVE SMARTER

scenes.text: Lesson number fourteen. They see taxes as one of their biggest expenses.
scenes.caption: LESSON 14

scenes.text: For many households, taxes, federal, state, local, payroll, property and sales, add up to one of the largest expenses in their lives, sometimes larger than housing. Yet most people spend far more time comparing grocery prices than understanding their taxes.
scenes.caption: ONE OF THE BIGGEST BILLS

scenes.text: Wealthy people manage taxes the way they manage any big expense. They look for legal ways to reduce it, plan ahead and track it. Saving a few percent on a huge expense can matter more than cutting many small ones.
scenes.caption: MANAGE IT LIKE AN EXPENSE

scenes.text: This isn't about avoiding your fair share. It's about using the rules Congress wrote, many of which were created specifically to encourage saving for retirement, health care, education and giving.
scenes.caption: USE THE RULES AS WRITTEN

scenes.text: Try this. Add up every tax you paid last year, including payroll, property and state taxes. Seeing the full number is often a wake up call.
scenes.caption: ADD UP EVERY TAX

scenes.text: That's angle two. After tax thinking, year round planning, paying for good advice, owning instead of just earning, patience, strategic giving and treating taxes as a big expense. Now angle three. The playbook.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: You don't need to be a billionaire to use tax advantages. Many of the most powerful ones were designed for ordinary workers. Here are six legal moves that can lower your taxes and help your money grow faster. Remember, rules and limits change every year, so check the current numbers with the IRS or a tax professional.
scenes.caption: SIX LEGAL MOVES

scenes.text: Move number fifteen. Use pre tax retirement accounts.
scenes.caption: LESSON 15

scenes.text: Contributions to a traditional four oh one k, and in many cases a traditional IRA, can reduce your taxable income this year. If you're in the twenty two percent federal bracket, every one thousand dollars you contribute could cut your federal income tax by about two hundred twenty dollars.
scenes.caption: LOWER TAXABLE INCOME

scenes.text: The money then grows tax deferred. You don't pay tax on dividends or gains each year, so more stays invested and compounding. You'll pay ordinary income tax when you withdraw it in retirement, ideally when your income and tax rate may be lower.
scenes.caption: TAX DEFERRED GROWTH

scenes.text: Add the employer match, and a pre tax four oh one k becomes one of the most powerful wealth building tools available to regular workers.
scenes.caption: PLUS THE MATCH

scenes.text: Try this. Increase your four oh one k contribution by one or two percent. Because it comes out before taxes, your take home pay falls by less than the amount you contribute.
scenes.caption: RAISE IT 1 TO 2%

scenes.text: Move number sixteen. Use Roth accounts for tax free growth.

card.title: Use a Roth for tax free growth

scenes.caption: LESSON 16
scenes.chapter: 16. Use a Roth for tax free growth

scenes.text: With a Roth IRA or Roth four oh one k, you contribute money you've already paid tax on. But qualified withdrawals in retirement, including all the growth, are tax free. For a young investor, decades of growth could never be taxed.
scenes.caption: TAX FREE GROWTH

scenes.text: Roth accounts are especially attractive when your tax rate today is lower than you expect it to be later, which is common early in a career. Many people use a mix of traditional and Roth accounts to keep flexibility in retirement.
scenes.caption: GREAT EARLY IN A CAREER

scenes.text: Roth IRAs have income limits for direct contributions and yearly contribution limits, so check the current IRS numbers. Roth four oh one k accounts, offered by many employers, don't have the same income limits.
scenes.caption: CHECK THE LIMITS

scenes.text: Try this. If you're eligible and don't have one, open a Roth IRA and set up even a small automatic monthly contribution.
scenes.caption: OPEN A ROTH

scenes.text: Move number seventeen. Use a health savings account if you can.
scenes.caption: LESSON 17

scenes.text: If you have a qualifying high deductible health plan, you may be able to contribute to a health savings account, or HSA. HSAs offer what's often called a triple tax advantage. Contributions can be tax deductible, growth is tax free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax free.
scenes.caption: TRIPLE TAX ADVANTAGE
scenes.short_hook: There's one account with a triple tax break, and most people ignore it.

scenes.text: Many people use their HSA like a checking account for medical bills. But some HSA providers let you invest the balance. If you can afford to pay current medical costs out of pocket and let the HSA grow, it can become a powerful long term account.
scenes.caption: INVEST YOUR HSA

scenes.text: After age sixty five, you can generally withdraw HSA money for non medical expenses too, paying ordinary income tax, similar to a traditional IRA. Medical withdrawals remain tax free at any age. Keep receipts, because qualified expenses can often be reimbursed later.
scenes.caption: KEEP YOUR RECEIPTS

scenes.text: Try this. Check whether your health plan is HSA eligible during open enrollment, and if you have an HSA, see whether you can invest the balance in low cost funds.
scenes.caption: CHECK ELIGIBILITY

scenes.text: Move number eighteen. Hold investments long term and know about the zero percent rate.
scenes.caption: LESSON 18

scenes.text: Long term capital gains and qualified dividends can be taxed at zero percent for people with taxable income below certain thresholds. Those thresholds are adjusted each year, and for many lower and middle income households, especially married couples, they're higher than people expect.
scenes.caption: THE 0% RATE EXISTS

scenes.text: That means some retirees and modest earners can sell investments with gains and owe no federal tax on those gains, as long as their taxable income stays within the bracket. Some people use low income years to realize gains on purpose.
scenes.caption: USE LOW INCOME YEARS

scenes.text: And for everyone, holding investments for more than a year before selling generally qualifies gains for the lower long term rates instead of ordinary income rates.
scenes.caption: HOLD OVER A YEAR

scenes.text: Try this. Look up the current long term capital gains brackets on the IRS website and see which rate applies to your taxable income.
scenes.caption: KNOW YOUR RATE

scenes.text: Move number nineteen. Use tax loss harvesting in taxable accounts.

card.title: Harvest your losses
card.sub: turn bad years into tax savings

scenes.caption: LESSON 19

scenes.text: If an investment in a regular taxable account has fallen below what you paid, you can sell it to realize a loss. That loss can offset capital gains, and if losses exceed gains, up to three thousand dollars a year can generally offset ordinary income. Extra losses can be carried forward to future years.
scenes.caption: LOSSES CAN OFFSET GAINS

scenes.text: Many investors then buy a similar, but not substantially identical, investment to stay invested in the market. That way they keep their market exposure while capturing the tax benefit.
scenes.caption: STAY INVESTED

scenes.text: Watch out for the wash sale rule. If you buy the same or a substantially identical investment within thirty days before or after the sale, the loss can be disallowed for now. Many brokerages track this, but it's your responsibility.
scenes.caption: THE WASH SALE RULE

scenes.text: Try this. Near the end of the year, review your taxable account for investments with losses, and consider whether harvesting them makes sense for your situation.
scenes.caption: YEAR END REVIEW

scenes.text: Move number twenty. Build income from ownership.
scenes.caption: LESSON 20

scenes.text: A real side business can open up legitimate deductions, like equipment, software, a portion of a home office if you qualify, and business mileage. Self employed people can also open retirement accounts like a SEP IRA or a solo four oh one k, which can allow larger contributions.
scenes.caption: A REAL SIDE BUSINESS

scenes.text: Rental real estate is another path, with depreciation and expense deductions. But it comes with real work, risk and rules, including limits on deducting rental losses for many taxpayers.
scenes.caption: REAL ESTATE HAS RULES

scenes.text: The goal isn't to start a business just for tax breaks. It's to build something that earns money, and then make sure you're using every legitimate deduction and account available to owners.
scenes.caption: EARN FIRST, THEN OPTIMIZE

scenes.text: Try this. If you have side income, track every legitimate business expense in a simple spreadsheet or app from day one, and keep business and personal money in separate accounts.
scenes.caption: TRACK FROM DAY ONE

scenes.text: In 2011, Warren Buffett wrote an opinion piece in The New York Times called Stop Coddling the Super Rich. He said that in 2010, the federal income and payroll taxes he paid were about seventeen point four percent of his taxable income. That was a lower percentage than any of the other twenty people in his office.
scenes.caption: BUFFETT'S 17.4%
scenes.short_hook: Warren Buffett said he paid a lower tax rate than his office staff.

scenes.text: According to Buffett, the tax burdens of his office staff ranged from thirty three to forty one percent, and averaged thirty six percent. The difference wasn't illegal tricks. Most of his income came from investments taxed at lower rates, while his staff mostly earned wages taxed at ordinary rates plus payroll taxes.
scenes.caption: STAFF PAID 33% TO 41%

scenes.text: Buffett argued that the rules should change. Whether you agree or not, his example shows the core lesson of this video. The tax code rewards owning assets more than earning wages. You can't change the code, but you can change the mix of your income over time by building ownership.
scenes.caption: THE CORE LESSON

scenes.text: Let's make this concrete with a simple example. Meet Sam, who earns seventy thousand dollars a year in salary and has never thought much about taxes. Here are three legal changes Sam could make. The exact savings depend on Sam's full situation, so treat these as rough illustrations.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Change one. Sam raises their four oh one k contribution from three percent to ten percent of salary. That's an extra four thousand nine hundred dollars a year going in before taxes. In the twenty two percent federal bracket, that could lower Sam's federal income tax by roughly one thousand dollars a year, while capturing more of the employer match and growing tax deferred.
scenes.caption: CHANGE 1: MORE PRE TAX SAVING

scenes.text: Change two. Sam switches to an HSA eligible health plan at open enrollment, after checking that it makes sense for their health needs, and contributes a few thousand dollars a year. Those contributions can also reduce taxable income, and if Sam invests the balance, it can grow tax free for future medical costs.
scenes.caption: CHANGE 2: AN HSA

scenes.text: Change three. Sam opens a Roth IRA and invests a few hundred dollars a month in a low cost index fund. No tax break today, but decades of growth that may never be taxed. Now Sam has pre tax money, tax free money and health money, which gives flexibility to manage taxes in retirement.
scenes.caption: CHANGE 3: A ROTH IRA

scenes.text: None of these changes required a higher income, a business or a team of advisors. Just a few forms and a little planning. That's how ordinary workers start using the same basic idea the wealthy use. Keep more, invest more, and let ownership grow over time.
scenes.caption: NO HIGHER INCOME REQUIRED

scenes.text: In your twenties and early career, your tax rate is often lower than it will be later. That can make Roth contributions especially attractive, because you pay tax now at a low rate and can withdraw growth tax free later. Always grab the employer match first.
scenes.caption: EARLY CAREER: THINK ROTH

scenes.text: In your peak earning years, pre tax contributions often become more valuable, because each dollar saved avoids a higher tax rate. This is also when HSAs, catch up contributions after fifty and careful year end planning can make the biggest difference.
scenes.caption: PEAK EARNING: THINK PRE TAX

scenes.text: Near and in retirement, planning shifts to withdrawals. Which accounts to draw from first, whether to convert some money to Roth in low income years, and how to manage required minimum distributions. A tax professional can be especially valuable here.
scenes.caption: RETIREMENT: PLAN WITHDRAWALS

scenes.text: Question one. Is this tax evasion? No. Tax avoidance means using legal rules to reduce taxes. Tax evasion means illegally hiding income or lying to the IRS. Everything in this video is about legal strategies. Evasion can lead to penalties and even criminal charges.
scenes.caption: AVOIDANCE VS EVASION

scenes.text: Question two. Do I need to be rich to use these strategies? No. Retirement accounts, Roth IRAs, HSAs, long term holding and the zero percent capital gains rate are available to millions of ordinary people. Many are most valuable for middle income households.
scenes.caption: NOT JUST FOR THE RICH

scenes.text: Question three. Should I choose traditional or Roth? It depends on whether you expect your tax rate to be higher now or in retirement. Many people split contributions between both for flexibility. A tax professional can help you decide.
scenes.caption: TRADITIONAL OR ROTH?

scenes.text: Question four. What about state taxes? States vary widely. Some have no income tax, some tax capital gains like regular income and some have special rules for retirement income. Check your state's rules, because they can change the math.
scenes.caption: STATE TAXES VARY

scenes.text: Question five. Will these rules change? Very possibly. Tax laws change regularly, and many proposals have targeted rules like the step up in basis, carried interest and the taxation of unrealized gains for the very wealthy. That's why it's smart to focus on durable habits, like saving in tax advantaged accounts and holding investments for the long term, and to review your plan every year as the rules evolve.
scenes.caption: WILL THE RULES CHANGE?

scenes.text: Mistake one. Skipping retirement accounts. Not using a four oh one k, IRA or HSA when you're eligible means paying more tax than you need to, year after year, and losing decades of tax advantaged growth.
scenes.caption: SKIPPING TAX ADVANTAGED ACCOUNTS
scenes.chapter: Tax mistakes that cost regular people

scenes.text: Mistake two. Selling too soon. Selling investments held one year or less can mean paying ordinary income rates on gains that might have qualified for lower long term rates with a little patience.
scenes.caption: SELLING TOO SOON

scenes.text: Mistake three. Cashing out a retirement account early. Withdrawals before age fifty nine and a half can trigger income tax plus a ten percent penalty in many cases, and the money loses all its future tax advantaged growth.
scenes.caption: CASHING OUT EARLY

scenes.text: Mistake four. Ignoring the tax on frequent trading in a taxable account. Every short term gain is taxed like a paycheck, and every trade is a new tax decision. Many people who think they're beating the market discover they're behind once taxes and costs are included. Buying and holding broad funds keeps taxes low and decisions simple.
scenes.caption: FREQUENT TRADING TAXES

scenes.text: Mistake five. Never checking beneficiaries and estate basics. Without updated beneficiaries and a simple will, families can face delays, legal costs and taxes that were avoidable. A few hours of planning can protect the step up in basis and make sure your money goes where you want.
scenes.caption: IGNORING ESTATE BASICS

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Two kinds of income, untaxed growth, borrowing, the step up in basis, payroll tax limits, business deductions and carried interest.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. After tax thinking, year round planning, good advice, ownership, patience, strategic giving and treating taxes as a big expense.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 8 TO 14

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. Pre tax accounts, Roth accounts, the HSA, long term holding, tax loss harvesting and ownership income.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 15 TO 20

scenes.text: The rich pay less tax mainly because of what kind of money they have. You can start shifting your own money in that direction, one paycheck at a time. If you want my full step by step plan, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments, which tax account are you going to use this year? I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
